content.body:
Its WWI tank heritage evident in the round-the-hull track and nestled hull gun, the Char B1 bis was nevertheless a sophisticated piece of equipment. The turret was exactly the same as used on the S-35, while the hull had a 75 mm howitzer style gun. Massive armor protected it from all directions, it was nearly impossible to kill with the regular or average AT guns. However, it had a number of drawbacks, such as the slow speed, poor communications, the usual French one-man turret, and an excessively complex transmission.
Surprisingly for a vehicle so comprehensively protected, the B1 had an Achilles' heel in its left engine grille, which most Germans didn’t discover until after the Battle of France was over. The Germans converted a number of captured B1s to flame tanks (some were used against British para's at Arnheim). The Free French recaptured others and employed them again against the Germans at the very end of the war.
Playing the B1 is an adventure. There are so many things to do that it is far more effective multi-crewed than any other vehicle. Because of its slow speed, you have a lot of time to familiarize yourself with the complicated control suite, quite different than other tanks although not too different for anyone familiar with French vehicles. The hull 75 mm is extremely inaccurate and has a slow Rate of Fire (ROF), so don't rely on blasting your way through anything with that. As the driver you must always be aware of that left grille. Knowledgeable German gunners in this game have had years of practice where the real ones barely had 4 weeks. It is now standard to shoot first at the right track of the B1 to cause the tank to turn and expose its radiator grille. Tracks are relatively easy to destroy and, if the B1 is moving shooting the right one will make it swing around to the right, exposing the vulnerable left radiator grille to the shooter.
When facing these clever fellows, your best response is simply to stop. Unlike almost every other tank, stopping in a Char is a perfectly reasonable tactic; your gun stability will improve and you can directly cope with any threats to your left side with the turret gun, while your armor shrugs off the hits.
Keep a close eye out for 88s though, they are a threat to you if you let them get close enough so spray them constantly with MG fire, you may get lucky and kill the gunner. Like all French tanks, make sure you do not accidentally open the gunner's port. On other tanks, this would leave a very small vulnerability in the mantlet; on French tanks it opens the a gaping port on the entire back of the turret leaving your turret members entirely exposed to even pistol fire.
Control Variations: This is a very distinct vehicle. The driver can zoom in the open view slit view (numpad 0 or Ins key) but has no periscope. He also controls the 75 mm hull gun and can use the gunsight with the numpad . or Del keys. However, the range on the sight cannot be adjusted. The gun's elevation is controlled from driver's position by with the I (up) and K (down) keys; the entire tank must be turned to adjust aiming left and right.
The commander is in a cupola and cannot unbutton, but he has an armored view slit (press O to open). The gunner controls 47 mm and Reibel MG in the turret. his viewport is BEHIND him (key O to open) and numpad 0 or Ins key to look and zoom.
The loader has no weapon, but can see a gauge that shows the direction the top turret is pointing relative to vehicle body. Use numpad 0 or Ins key to zoom in on gauge.
